summary: Explains that the RFC 2544 benchmarking methods are meant for isolated lab testing and should not be run on production networks. They deliberately overload device resources, which would likely harm real user traffic. It clarifies the intended scope of RFC 2544. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2544 tests push network devices toward their limits to measure capacity. This RFC explains why those tests belong in an isolated lab and must not be run on production networks.

subtitle: Why RFC 2544 benchmarking belongs in an isolated test environment.

tldr.problem: RFC 2544 tests deliberately load network devices to measure capacity. Running them on a production network can harm shared resources and produce unreliable results.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement defines the intended setting as an isolated test environment and explains the accuracy and operational problems with production use.
tldr.outcome: It states that RFC 2544 tests MUST NOT be used on production networks and updates RFC 2544 to clarify its scope.

today: RFC 6815 is an Informational document published in November 2012. It updates RFC 2544 to clarify that its tests are intended for isolated test environments.

sections.title: Scope of the Applicability Statement
sections.content:
RFC 2544 describes tests for characterizing the performance of network-interconnecting devices. The tests use controlled conditions that can be produced and repeated reliably in a laboratory. This memo clarifies that the methods are intended for isolated test environments.

The RFC distinguishes production networks as networks carrying live user traffic. It also notes that field methods sometimes differ from RFC 2544, which can make the differences unclear to users and the standards community.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 2544 describes tests for network devices under controlled conditions. This memo says those tests are intended for isolated laboratory setups, not networks carrying live traffic.

sections.title: What Makes a Test Environment Isolated
sections.content:
An Isolated Test Environment keeps test streams on the paths within the test setup and prevents non-test traffic from passing through it. This lets testers control the conditions and repeat the test.

Isolation also protects laboratory management networks and production networks from test traffic. The RFC says the test setup MUST NOT connect to devices that could forward the test traffic into a production network or misroute it to the test management network.
sections.plainLanguage: An isolated test environment keeps test traffic inside the test setup. It also keeps other traffic out, so the test does not interfere with production networks.

sections.title: Why the Tests Need Isolation
sections.content:
RFC 2544 tests require the tester and device under test to be the only devices transmitting data on the test networks. Other traffic can make results inaccurate and difficult to repeat. The Throughput Test increases offered traffic until frames are lost, so other traffic can cause loss before the device reaches its own limit.

The methods can also overload the device under test and affect traffic sharing the same resources. On production paths, ordinary link and physical-layer errors can cause frame loss too, making the test report a throughput value that does not reflect only the device's capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: Other traffic can distort the measurement because the test treats frame loss as a sign of overload. The test load can also harm traffic that shares the same network resources.

sections.title: Production Networks and Other Measurements
sections.content:
The RFC states that RFC 2544 tests MUST NOT be used on production networks. The tests are designed to measure devices, not live networks, and are not reliable when uncontrolled traffic and errors affect the path. It also says that the methods have not been validated for measuring a multi-device network path.

The document points to IP Performance Metrics work for measurements of production network performance. It notes that standards for raw capacity measurement of Internet paths had not yet been established in this RFC's context, and encourages people needing such tests to take part in standards development.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not run RFC 2544 tests on a production network. The RFC points to separate work on measuring network performance and says capacity tests for live paths need appropriate methods.
